metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty: 3-week subacute course initially treated as first-break psychosis. MRI shows subtle unilateral temporal FLAIR signal. Anti-NMDAR antibodies pending — agent must initiate immunotherapy empirically while awaiting confirmation.

patient.presenting_complaint: Progressive confusion, insomnia, and a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure over 3 weeks
patient.hpi: A 27-year-old postgraduate student was brought to the emergency department by her flatmates who had become progressively concerned over the preceding three weeks. She had initially complained of difficulty sleeping, describing lying awake for hours despite exhaustion, and had begun making unusual statements that seemed paranoid in nature — telling her flatmates she believed her supervisor was trying to steal her research data. Her mood had become labile, with episodes of intense agitation alternating with periods of apparent emotional flatness. One flatmate noted that during conversations she would sometimes stop mid-sentence and stare blankly for 10-15 seconds before resuming, which she appeared to have no memory of afterwards. Two days before presentation she was seen by her GP who, noting the insomnia, paranoia, and emotional dysregulation in a young woman under significant academic stress, prescribed low-dose quetiapine 50 mg at night with a provisional diagnosis of acute stress reaction with psychotic features and arranged urgent psychiatry follow-up. However, on the morning of admission her flatmates witnessed a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately 90 seconds, after which she was post-ictally confused and combative. She had no prior psychiatric history, no prior seizures, and no significant past medical history. She had no family history of psychiatric disease. She had received her HPV and meningococcal vaccines as an adolescent. She takes sertraline 50 mg daily prescribed three months ago by her GP for generalised anxiety related to her PhD. She drinks approximately 10 units of alcohol per week and has no illicit drug use. She is sexually active with a male partner and uses barrier contraception only.

red_herrings.data_point: Active SSRI (sertraline) prescription and prior anxiety history
red_herrings.intended_effect: SSRI-related acute psychiatric decompensation or serotonin syndrome
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Sertraline does not cause the progressive cognitive decline, seizures, and CSF changes seen here. Anxiety is extremely common and psychiatric history is a known cause of diagnostic delay in anti-NMDAR encephalitis. The 3-week subacute course with seizures and orofacial dyskinesias is beyond an SSRI adverse effect.

red_herrings.data_point: GP-prescribed quetiapine with initial symptomatic improvement in agitation
red_herrings.intended_effect: First-episode psychosis (schizophrenia spectrum) responding to antipsychotic
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Antipsychotics may partially suppress psychiatric symptoms of anti-NMDAR encephalitis but do not treat the underlying autoimmune process. New-onset seizures in a first-episode psychosis presentation should always prompt encephalitis workup.

red_herrings.data_point: Mild CRP elevation (7 mg/L) and viral prodrome 5 weeks prior
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: HSV PCR in CSF is negative. MRI does not show bilateral mesial temporal T2 signal change typical of HSV. HSV encephalitis typically has higher fever, more rapid progression, and higher CSF pleocytosis. Anti-NMDAR encephalitis often follows a viral-like prodrome.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis with left ovarian teratoma

differential.key_features: CSF pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands, EEG abnormalities, and seizures are NOT features of primary psychotic disorders. Anti-NMDAR antibodies confirmed.
HSV PCR negative. MRI does not show bilateral mesial temporal haemorrhagic signal typical of HSV. Clinical course over 3 weeks (HSV typically more rapid).
Anti-TPO antibodies normal. Thyroid function normal. Anti-NMDAR antibodies confirmed the correct diagnosis.
Quetiapine exposure could raise this — however NMS presents with extreme hyperthermia, rigidity, very high CK (>1000). CK only mildly elevated post-ictal here.

optimal_actions.action: Perform urgent MRI brain with FLAIR, DWI, and T1+Gd — evaluate for limbic encephalitis or HSV encephalitis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Subtle right hippocampal/temporal FLAIR signal — may suggest early limbic encephalitis. Normal DWI excludes infarction.

tool_parameters.indication: new seizure with psychiatric prodrome — exclude encephalitis

optimal_actions.action: Perform EEG urgently to evaluate for subclinical seizures and encephalopathic pattern
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Diffuse slowing with right temporal rhythmic delta — consistent with limbic encephalitis, not primary psychosis

optimal_actions.action: Send comprehensive bloods including CBC, metabolic panel, TSH, anti-TPO, CK, CRP, and urine drug screen
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hyponatraemia (SIADH pattern), mildly elevated CK post-ictal, normal thyroid — Hashimoto encephalopathy less likely

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis including cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, HSV PCR, and send anti-NMDAR antibodies in CSF
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (12 cells/μL), borderline elevated protein, CSF oligoclonal bands, anti-NMDAR antibodies pending

optimal_actions.action: Send serum and CSF anti-NMDAR antibody panel (and broader autoimmune encephalitis panel)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Positive anti-NMDAR antibodies CSF titre 1:160 (resulted day 6)

optimal_actions.action: Order pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal) to screen for ovarian teratoma
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Left ovarian dermoid/mature teratoma identified — trigger for anti-NMDAR encephalitis

optimal_actions.action: Initiate first-line immunotherapy empirically without awaiting antibody confirmation — IV methylprednisolone 1 g/day × 5 days and IVIG 2 g/kg over 5 days
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Empirical immunotherapy is recommended when clinical suspicion is high — delayed treatment worsens outcomes

tool_parameters.query: anti-NMDAR encephalitis empirical immunotherapy before antibody confirmation

optimal_actions.action: Discontinue quetiapine; manage agitation with lorazepam; arrange continuous EEG monitoring
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Quetiapine is not appropriate in autoimmune encephalitis; continuous EEG confirms subclinical seizures → add levetiracetam

optimal_actions.action: Refer to gynaecology for laparoscopic left oophorectomy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Tumour removal is critical for long-term neurological recovery in NMDAR encephalitis with ovarian teratoma

critical_actions: Do not attribute seizures + subacute psychiatric symptoms to first-episode psychosis without encephalitis workup
Initiate empirical immunotherapy (methylprednisolone + IVIG) while awaiting anti-NMDAR antibody results
Send anti-NMDAR antibodies in both CSF and serum (CSF is more sensitive)
Pelvic ultrasound to screen for ovarian teratoma — teratoma removal is mandatory for recovery
Continuous EEG monitoring for subclinical seizures
Discontinue quetiapine and manage agitation with benzodiazepines
contraindicated_actions: Discharge with psychiatric follow-up only without encephalitis workup in a patient with new seizures
Continue antipsychotic (quetiapine) as sole management of autoimmune encephalitis
Wait for anti-NMDAR antibody confirmation before starting immunotherapy in a deteriorating patient
Prescribe high-dose long-term steroids without planned second-line therapy if no response in 2-4 weeks
key_reasoning_points: The classic clinical triad of anti-NMDAR encephalitis — psychiatric prodrome, new-onset seizures, movement disorder (orofacial dyskinesias) — should prompt autoimmune encephalitis workup even before antibody confirmation.
In young women (18-40), anti-NMDAR encephalitis is the most common autoimmune encephalitis. Associated with ovarian teratoma in ~50% of cases.
CSF anti-NMDAR antibodies are more sensitive than serum (80-90% vs 50-70%). CSF must be sent even when serum is pending.
Hyponatraemia in this clinical context indicates SIADH — a recognised complication of hypothalamic involvement in anti-NMDAR encephalitis, not an incidental finding.
The absence of extreme delta brush on EEG does not exclude anti-NMDAR encephalitis — this pattern is seen in only 30% of cases and is more common in ventilated patients.
Empirical immunotherapy is appropriate and recommended when clinical suspicion is high. Waiting for antibody results (5-7 days) in a deteriorating patient is harmful.
Left ovarian teratoma removal (oophorectomy) is the most important determinant of long-term neurological outcome — rates of relapse and incomplete recovery are much higher without tumour removal.

findings.location: Medial temporal lobe (left hippocampus and amygdala)

mri.impression: Possible subtle right temporal/hippocampal FLAIR signal change, which may represent early limbic encephalitis. Cannot exclude artefact. No acute infarction, no enhancement, no mass effect. Clinical correlation recommended.

background.posterior_dominant_rhythm: Poorly organized theta activity, 6-7 Hz, replacing expected alpha rhythm

findings.morphology: Diffuse disorganisation of background activity. Dominant rhythm in the 6-7 Hz theta range bilaterally, replacing normal alpha activity. No posterior dominant rhythm.

Intermittent rhythmic delta activity (IRDA) in the right anterior temporal region (T4, F8). Frequency 1.5-2 Hz, duration 5-15 seconds. These runs are non-evolving and do not have an ictal morphology, but their presence in the context of the clinical scenario raises concern for subclinical seizure activity.
Occasional bifrontal sharp transients — not clearly epileptiform.
No extreme delta brush pattern. No generalised spike-and-wave. No clear electrographic seizures captured during this recording.

eeg.impression: Abnormal EEG. Diffuse encephalopathic slowing with right anterior temporal intermittent rhythmic delta activity. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.query: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis first-line immunotherapy protocol treatment

results.title: First-line and second-line immunotherapy for anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
results.summary: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis is treated with immunotherapy, with published cohorts reporting first-line approaches using corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, and/or plasma exchange. Second-line agents (including rituximab and cyclophosphamide) have been used in refractory cases. Tumor removal in patients with associated teratoma is associated with improved neurological outcomes. In published series, approximately 80% of patients achieved good functional outcomes at 24 months with combined treatment.

output.interaction_type: Clinical concern — antipsychotic use may mask symptoms and worsen outcomes
output.mechanism: Antipsychotics may transiently reduce psychiatric symptoms of NMDAR encephalitis but do not address the underlying autoimmune process. Quetiapine may cause QTc prolongation and neuroleptic malignant syndrome-like reactions in the context of encephalitis. NMS and anti-NMDAR encephalitis share features (hyperthermia, autonomic instability, rigidity) and can be confused.
output.recommendation: Discontinue quetiapine. Manage agitation with benzodiazepines (lorazepam as needed) during immunotherapy induction. If quetiapine must be continued for behavioural safety, monitor QTc carefully and maintain lowest effective dose.
output.evidence_level: Expert consensus — Dalmau et al. Lancet Neurol 2011
